analysis.one_liner: Replaces jury trials for malpractice cases with state arbitration panels and caps pain-and-suffering awards at $250,000.
analysis.headline: Introduced in July 1989 with 15 cosponsors from both parties, the bill was sent to two House committees, never received a hearing or vote, and expired when the 101st Congress ended in January 1991.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have offered states federal money (at least $100 million a year) if they set up medical malpractice arbitration panels that would take over every malpractice claim in the state, replacing jury trials. The panels could award at most $250,000 for pain and suffering, would subtract any other compensation a patient received from the award, and would cap lawyers' fees. It also included pro-patient measures: panels had to report findings of negligence to state licensing boards and insurance regulators, states had to run programs to prevent medical errors, and doctors found negligent could face higher insurance rates and discipline.
analysis.who_benefits: Doctors, hospitals, and medical malpractice insurers would gain the most. Moving all claims to panels, capping pain-and-suffering damages at $250,000, subtracting other compensation from awards, limiting attorney fees, and letting panels charge plaintiffs up to $10,000 for claims dismissed as frivolous would all cut malpractice payouts and, in turn, insurance premiums [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Panels would have original and exclusive jurisdiction over all malpractice claims except those against the federal government, meaning injured patients could not take their case to a jury first [S2][S3].

Noneconomic (pain-and-suffering) damages would be capped at $250,000, adjusted for inflation every three years, and awards would be reduced by any compensation received from other sources such as health insurance [S2][S3].
A sliding fee schedule would cap attorneys' fees (33% on awards up to $100,000, dropping to 15% on amounts above $300,000), and attorneys who charged more would owe triple the excess [S2][S3].
Panels could dismiss claims they found frivolous and impose up to $10,000 in administrative costs on the plaintiff [S3].

The bill also required panels to report negligence findings and settlements to state licensing boards and insurance commissioners, made those reports public, and let states authorize insurers to raise rates on doctors found negligent or with repeated settlements [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Injured patients would bear the cost: their cases would go to a panel instead of a jury, their pain-and-suffering recovery would be capped, their awards reduced by other insurance they had paid for, and the most severely injured would lose the most relative to what a jury could award.

drawbacks.text: A flat $250,000 cap on pain and suffering falls hardest on the worst-injured patients — a child facing lifelong disability from a birth injury has the same cap as someone with a minor injury [S3].
The collateral source offset forces patients to give up the value of health insurance or disability benefits they already paid for, reducing their total recovery [S2][S3].
Exclusive panel jurisdiction and a possible $10,000 penalty for claims dismissed as frivolous could deter valid claims, especially from families who cannot afford the risk [S3].
Decisions by the Attorney General to deny, terminate, or reallocate state funding would be final and not subject to judicial review [S3].

Supporters would argue that malpractice lawsuits drive up defensive medicine costs and premiums, and that faster panel decisions with mandatory reporting of negligent doctors could improve patient safety — real benefits the bill pursued alongside the liability limits [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill bundled two things together: real limits on patients' compensation (caps, offsets, fee limits, forced arbitration) and genuine patient-safety measures (public reporting of negligent doctors, error-prevention programs, discipline). The liability limits — the bill's center of gravity — would transfer the most from the most severely injured patients to doctors and their insurers, while the safety provisions could have been enacted without the caps.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced with 15 cosponsors and referred to the Judiciary and Energy and Commerce committees, it was passed down to two subcommittees, never got a hearing or a vote, and expired when the 101st Congress ended in January 1991 [S5].

narrative.text: Rep. Robert Mrazek (D-NY) introduced the bill on July 11, 1989, joined by 15 cosponsors — 7 Democrats and 8 Republicans [S1][S4][S5].
The House referred it jointly to the Judiciary and Energy and Commerce committees on the day of introduction [S5].
Within three weeks it was sent to the Judiciary Subcommittee on Economic and Commercial Law (July 17) and the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health and the Environment (July 31) [S5].
No further action appears in the record; the bill died in subcommittee when the Congress ended on January 3, 1991 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Injured patients kept full access to jury trials and uncapped jury awards, because the bill never advanced. Doctors and insurers gained nothing, but also lost nothing — the malpractice system stayed as it was.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Injured patients kept their jury-trial rights

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was evenly split between parties (7 Democrats, 8 Republicans), and the bill died in committee without any recorded vote, so no party-line split ever showed up on the record.

industries.note: Damage caps, the collateral source offset, fee limits, and panel dismissal of claims would all reduce what insurers pay out, and the bill would have given them rate-setting leverage over doctors found negligent. Insurers' savings come directly out of compensation owed to injured patients.

The bill's liability limits — forced arbitration, a $250,000 pain-and-suffering cap, capped attorney fees — would shield providers from large jury awards and could lower premiums. But the same bill would have exposed negligent doctors to public reports to licensing boards, possible discipline, and higher insurance rates.

A mandatory fee schedule (capped as low as 15% on large awards), installment payment of fees, and treble damages for overcharging would cut contingent-fee income. Lawyers' interest here runs with patients seeking full compensation.
